newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court overrides German awards for sex discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Court overrides German awards for sex discrimination.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Tuesday that member states may not limit damage awards for discriminatory hiring on the basis of sex.
The court's decision strikes down a German law which caps damages at a rate of three months' salary for a clear convincing case of sex discrimination in the hiring process.
If an employer can prove the successful applicant in the hiring process was more qualified, damages for the applicant denied a postion may be limited to three months, the court said.
The court also ruled out the requirement that fault be proved to make a case of discrimination, under EU rules.

Although German law on fault allows liability for deliberate or negligent acts, the court said "the directive does not make liability on the part of the person guilty of discrimination conditional on proof of fault or on the absence of any ground discharging such liability."
This is the second ruling from Germany that has broken ground in the area of sex discrimination awards in the work place, and both have been initiated by men.

The first "reverse discrimination" claim was made by Eckhard Kalanke after he was passed over for a senior position with the Bremen city parks department, even though he was considered to be as qualified for the job as the woman who was hired.
The court in Kalanke struck down a German law guaranteeing absolute and unconditional priority for women in the workplace because it violated EU rules of equal employment.
In the current case, a man answered a job advert that specifically asked for a woman. Nils Draehmpaehl initiated a claim for sex discrimination when the employer did not respond to his application.
Nils Draehmpaehl and Urania Immobilienservice ohG

on the interpretation of Council directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976 on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment (OJ 1976 L 39, p. 40)

1. When a member state chooses to penalize, under rules governing civil liability, breach of the prohibiton of discrimination, Council directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976 on the implementationof the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment and in particular articles 2(1) and 3(1) thereof, preclude provisions of domestic law which make reparation of damage suffered as a result of discrimination on grounds of sex in the making of an appointment subject to the requirement of fault.

2. Directive 76/207 does not preclude provisions of domestic law hich prescribe an upper limit of three months' salary for the amount of compensation which may be claimed by an applicant where the employer can prove that, because the applicant engaged had superior qualifications, the unsuccessful applicant would not have obtained the vacant positon even if there had been no discrimination in the selection process. In contrast, the directive precludes provisions of domestic law which, unlike other provisions of domestic civil and labour law, presecribe an upper limit of three months's salary for the amount of compensation which may be claimed by an applicant discriminated against on grounds of sex in the making of an appointment where that applicant would have obtained the vacant position of the selection process had been carried out without discrimination.

3. Directive 76/207 does not preclude provisions of domestic law which, unlike other provisions of domestic civil and labour law, impose a ceiling of six months' earnings on the aggregate amount of compensation which, where several applicants claim compensation, may be calimed by applicants who have been discriminated against on grounds of their sex in the making of an appointment.
